communityWitnessing.subtitle: How to safely document ICE/DHS activity as a bystander witness
communityWitnessing.homeCardDesc: Etale bwebwenato in ICE ñan jipañ
communityWitnessing.legalCitationText: Glik v. Cunniff (1st Cir. 2011) and Fields v. City of Philadelphia (3rd Cir. 2017) confirm the First Amendment right to record government agents performing their duties in public.
communityWitnessing.roleBody: Community witnesses serve a vital legal function. When you document an ICE encounter, you create a record that attorneys and families can use. Your calm, steady presence is a form of protection — research shows agents are more likely to follow procedure when documented by witnesses.
communityWitnessing.positioningBody: Stand far enough to observe clearly without interfering. If you can read badge numbers and see what is happening, you are close enough.
communityWitnessing.posRule1: Stay on public property — sidewalks, streets, public parks
communityWitnessing.posRule2: If asked to step back, comply — document the request
communityWitnessing.posRule3: Rule of thumb: if you can see it clearly, you are close enough
communityWitnessing.posRule4: Never block a vehicle, doorway, or agent's path
communityWitnessing.documentSubtitle: Tap to check off — capture in priority order
communityWitnessing.doc1: Agency name (ICE / CBP / Border Patrol / local police)
communityWitnessing.doc2: Badge numbers and agent names if visible
communityWitnessing.doc4: Number of agents and number of vehicles
communityWitnessing.doc6: Whether agents showed a warrant — and what type
communityWitnessing.doc7: Detained person's name and country of origin if communicated
communityWitnessing.doc8: Uniform patches and insignia (agency matters for legal routing)
communityWitnessing.pipelineBody: The most powerful thing a witness can do is capture the detained person's name. ICE can move people across facilities within hours — a name is how family and attorneys find them.
communityWitnessing.pipelineStep1: Get the detained person's name — ask if you can safely do so
communityWitnessing.pipelineStep2: Note their country of origin or citizenship if communicated
communityWitnessing.pipelineStep3: Use ICE Detainee Locator (ice.gov/detainee-locator) to find which facility they are in
communityWitnessing.pipelineStep4: Share name and facility info with their family or attorney
communityWitnessing.pipelineStep5: Use Get Legal Help to connect with immigration attorneys immediately
communityWitnessing.pipelineNote: The ICE detainee locator may not update for 12–24 hours after detention. Keep checking.
communityWitnessing.agentsBody: You are not required to speak to agents. If they approach, you have one sentence.
communityWitnessing.agentsScript: I am observing from a public space and exercising my First Amendment rights.
communityWitnessing.agentsNote: Say nothing further. Remain calm. You are not required to identify yourself in most states when you are a witness, not a suspect.
communityWitnessing.witnessPartyTitle: Witness vs. Party — Know the Difference
communityWitnessing.witnessPartyBody: Your role is documentation, not intervention. If you speak to the detained person, hand them items, or physically intervene, you risk an obstruction charge.
communityWitnessing.stoicBody: Your emotional regulation is your greatest tool. Record steadily. Keep your face neutral. Do not engage agents in debate. You serve the detained person best by staying legally clean.
communityWitnessing.stoicQuote: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
communityWitnessing.offlineNote: All guide content works offline. No internet required.

legal.cdRightToAssemble: Jouj ñan Assemble: First Amendment ej protect jouj in armij ko ñan peacefully assemble. Ne ej include march ko, sit-in ko, vigil ko, rally ko, im tok form ko in collective expression ilo public property.

legal.cdFreedomOfSpeech: Freedom in Ba: Peaceful protest ej juon form in protected ba. Sign ko, chant ko, leaflet ko, im symbolic expression (kōn armband ko ilo silent vigil ko) rej wōt constitutionally protected activity ko.
legal.caseNaacp: NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware (1982): Supreme Court ej ruled bwe nonviolent element ko in juon protest (boycott ko, march ko, ba ko) rej constitutionally protected even ne jān participant ko rej engage ilo violence. Peaceful participant ko ejjeḷọk ad held liable ñan tok action ko.
legal.caseEdwards: Edwards v. South Carolina (1963): Court eo ej overturned conviction ko in 187 Black student ko arrested ñan peacefully protesting segregation ilo state capitol. Peaceful protest ilo public ground ko ej protected kōn 1st im 14th Amendment ko.
legal.caseTinker: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969): Court eo ej held bwe wearing black armband ko ñan protest Vietnam War ej protected symbolic ba. "Student ko rej ejjeḷọk shed rūtto constitutional jouj ko ilo schoolhouse gate."
legal.caseCox: Cox v. Louisiana (1965): Court eo ej ruled bwe peaceful picketing im parading rej protected form ko in expression. Ak, government eo ekatakin impose reasonable taim, jikin, im manner restriction ko.
legal.cdGenerallyProtected: Generally Protected: Marching ilo sidewalk ko im public jikin ko, holding sign ko, chanting, leafleting, silent vigil ko, boycott ko, human chain ko ilo public property, symbolic ba (armband ko, flag ko).
legal.cdMayCrossLines: Ekatakin Cross Legal Line Ko: Blocking road ko ilo entrance ko, occupying private property, refusing ñan disperse ke lawful order, interfering ilo government operation ko. Ne act ko in ekatakin result ilo arrest — know potential consequence ko einwōt participating.
legal.movementCivilRights: Civil Rights Movement (1950s-60s): Lunch counter sit-in ko, Freedom Ride ko, Montgomery Bus Boycott, im March ilo Washington used nonviolent civil disobedience ñan challenge segregation im secure Civil Rights Act in 1964 im Voting Rights Act in 1965.
legal.movementSuffrage: Women's Suffrage (1848-1920): Suffragist ko organized march ko, picket line ko ilo White House, im hunger strike ko. Rellọk rej arrested im imprisoned einwōt 19th Amendment ej ratified.
legal.movementLabor: Labor Movement (1880s-1940s): Strike ko, sit-down ko, im picket line ko fought ñan 8-hour workday, workplace safety, im jouj ñan organize. Ne action ko in led ñan National Labor Relations Act im Fair Labor Standards Act.
legal.movementSanctuary: Sanctuary Movement (1980s-present): Church ko im community ko rej katakin provided sanctuary ñan refugee ko im undocumented immigrant ko, drawing ilo religious im moral tradition ko in offering refuge ñan rūtto facing persecution.

legal.chargeTrespassing: Trespassing: Entering ilo remaining ilo property ejjeḷọk permission. Common ilo sit-in ko ilo building occupation ko. Typically juon misdemeanor. Penalty ko rej vary kōn state ak often include fine ko in $100-$1,000 im up ñan 30 raan ilo jail. legal.chargeDisorderlyConduct: Disorderly Conduct: Juon broad, catch-all charge often used ilo protest ko. Typically cover "disturbing peace eo," "unreasonable noise," ilo "tumultuous behavior." Ne ej most common protest arrest charge. Usually juon misdemeanor ilo fine ko im possible short jail taim. Ne charge ko in rej frequently dropped ilo dismissed.
legal.chargeUnlawfulAssembly: Unlawful Assembly: Ke authority ko rej declare juon gathering unlawful — typically ke rūtto rej determine ne ej pose juon "clear im present danger" in violence ilo property destruction. Juon formal dispersal order ej aikuj given einwōt ne charge in ej apply. Kwōj aikuj given juon reasonable opportunity ñan leave.
legal.chargeFailureToDisperse: Failure ñan Disperse: Remaining ke juon lawful dispersal order ej given. Order eo ej aikuj audible im clear. Kwōj aikuj given juon reasonable amount in taim ñan leave. Ne exit route ko rej blocked kōn police, ne ekatakin juon defense. Dokumeñto taim eo order eo ej given im whether kwōj ewōr juon clear path ñan leave.
legal.chargeObstruction: Obstruction / Resisting Arrest: Physically interfering ilo juon officer ilo resisting juon lawful arrest. Simply going limp (passive resistance) ekatakin ilo ejjeḷọk ad constitute resisting depending ilo state law. Verbal challenge ko ñan police rej generally protected ba. Ak, federal charge ko ekatakin apply ilo federal property (courthouse ko, federal building ko, national park ko), ke crossing state line ko ñan incite juon riot (Anti-Riot Act), ilo ke protest ko target federal operation ko. legal.safetyKnowLocalLaws: Know Local Law Ko: Research permit requirement ko, local curfew law ko, im wōt specific ordinance ko. Know ia eo jikin ko rej public property vs. private. Understand am state specific law ko ilo unlawful assembly im failure ñan disperse.
legal.safetyDeescalation: De-escalation: Remain calm im non-threatening. Jeramon̄ hand ko visible. Ba ilo calm, steady voice. Jab katakin sudden movement ko. Comply ilo lawful order ko ke verbally asserting am jouj ko.
legal.safetyDocumentEverything: Dokumeñto Wōt Men: Jipañ video ke safe ñan katakin ne (ne ej am First Amendment jouj). Note badge number ko, agency eta ko, vehicle number ko, im timestamp ko. Ne kwōj witness misconduct, lukkuun contact information jen tok witness ko.

legal.philosophyStoicDuty: Stoic Duty ñan Community: Stoic ko taught bwe jet ej citizen ko in world eo first, im bwe justice ej demand action — ejjeḷọk mere observation. Marcus Aurelius wrote: "Men eo ej ejjeḷọk kōṃṃan ñan bee-hive eo, ejjeḷọk ad kōṃṃan ñan bee eo." Epictetus taught bwe power ko in organizing whole eo rej ilo-within wōt armij eo. Ke law ko rej harm community eo, Stoic philosophy ej hold bwe conscience im duty ñan tok ko ekatakin call ñan principled action.
legal.philosophyThoreau: Henry David Thoreau — "Civil Disobedience" (1849): Thoreau argued bwe individual ko rej ewōr juon duty ñan katakin rūtto conscience over unjust law ko. Ej etal̗ ñan jail einwōt pay juon tax supporting slavery im Mexican-American War. Ne essay eo became foundational text in nonviolent resistance, directly influencing Gandhi im King.
legal.philosophyKing: Martin Luther King Jr. — Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963): King distinguished ilo-between just im unjust law ko: "Juon just law ej juon man-made code eo ej square ilo moral law eo. Juon unjust law ej juon code eo ej out in harmony ilo moral law eo." Ej argued bwe nonviolent direct action ej create tension eo necessary ñan change, im bwe rūtto eo rej break unjust law ko ej aikuj katakin ne "openly, lovingly, im ilo willingness ñan accept penalty eo."
legal.philosophyGandhi: Mahatma Gandhi — Satyagraha: Gandhi philosophy in "truth-force" ilo "soul-force" held bwe nonviolent resistance ej most powerful weapon against injustice. Ne principle ko: jab harm am opponent, accept suffering ejjeḷọk retaliation, always truthful, im recognize humanity eo ilo am adversary. Salt March in 1930 demonstrated kōn ad mass civil disobedience ekatakin shift public consciousness.
legal.philosophyCommonThread: Common Thread Eo: Gen Stoic ko ñan Thoreau ñan King ñan Gandhi, tradition in civil disobedience ej rest ilo juon shared conviction: bwe individual ko rej ewōr juon moral obligation ñan act ke law ko ilo system ko rej cause harm ñan tok ko, im bwe nonviolent action — undertaken openly im ilo acceptance in consequence ko — ej most powerful force ñan justice.

faq.generalA1: SafeNeighbor ej juon web platform eo ej kōm̧m̧ane bwe anemkwōj en m̧oktata, ej jipañ community ko kōn report ko kōn anemkwōj ilo iien eo wōt im̧ katak kōn civil rights. Kōm̧ kōlet tools ko ñan ri-jerbal ko an law im̧ legal scripts ko ñan iien ko eḷap pressure ie.

Report ṇe ej pād ñan ri-kōjerbal ro jet ilo area eo, im men in ej jipañ neighbors bwe ren kōm̧m̧ane informed decisions kōn travel im̧ anemkwōj eo aer ilo iien eo wōt. Identity eṃ ejjab attach ñan jabdewōt report — ejjelok account, ejjelok IP logging, im ejjelok precise GPS coordinates rej store. Report locations rej generalize ñan juon neighborhood-level radius im encrypt mokta jān rej leave device eṃ, im men in ej kōm̧m̧ane bwe ejjab maroñ trace juon report ñan armej eo ear submit e.

faq.privacyA2: Kōm̧ ej jab follow eok. Ñe app eo ej kōjerbal GPS eo an device eṃ ñan kōkḷap local reports, data ṇe ej jerbal locally ilo phone eṃ. Kōm̧ ej jab store juon history in movements aṃ ilo servers ko am̧.

Reports ko rej encrypted ilo device eṃ m̧okta jān aer bar jilkinl̗o̧k ñan database eo am̧. Ñe kōm̧ ar bok juon subpoena, kōm̧ ejjeḷọk wōt personal user data ñan letok bwe kōm̧ ar jab collect e jān m̧oktaṃ.
